units.title: The Sense Organs
units.intro:
Receptors turn a stimulus into a nerve impulse. Skin: touch, pressure, pain, temperature. Nose: chemoreceptors in the air stream. Tongue: taste buds (sweet, salt, sour, bitter — umami may be named). Eye: cornea + lens focus on the retina; rods = dim/black-white; cones = colour in bright light; iris controls pupil. Ear: pinna → canal → drum → ossicles → cochlea (hearing) and semicircular canals (balance).

Internal receptors watch stretch, blood chemistry, posture — they feed homeostasis in Grade 11.

cards.title: More detail — eye and ear
body: Eye path: cornea does most of the bending, lens does the fine focus (accommodation: fat lens for near, thin for far). Iris circular and radial muscles set pupil size. Blind spot = optic nerve exit, no receptors. Short sight: long eyeball, image in front of retina, diverging lens. Long sight: short eyeball or stiff lens, converging lens.

Ear path: air waves → drum → three bones amplify → oval window → fluid in cochlea → hair cells → auditory nerve. Semicircular canals detect rotation (fluid lag). Eustachian tube equalises pressure with the throat.

cards.title: 7.1.1 The Skin
body: The skin is the sense organ which covers the whole body.
For example the fingertips, lips and cheeks have the greatest concentration of receptors and are, therefore, more sensitive to their respective stimuli.
Skin receptors receive a signal and transmit it via nerve cells to the brain.
In the brain, the signals are interpreted as sensations.

cards.title: 7.1.2 The Nose
body: The nasal cavity is lined with mucous membranes that have smell receptors, which are connected to the olfactory nerve.
The smell itself consists of vapours of various substances.
The smell receptors are sensitive to different types of sensations and interact with the molecules of various vapours, transmitting the sensations to the brain through the olfactory bulb.
The chemical molecules of any odorous substance that enter the nose dissolve in the mucus and stimulate the olfactory receptors.

cards.title: 7.1.3 The Tongue
body: The tongue is a sense organ that helps identify taste.
The human tongue is dotted with thousands of taste buds, which are made up of many receptor cells.
Many of the taste buds are found in large swellings, called papillae.
Generally, the taste buds close to the tip of the tongue are sensitive to sweet tastes, whereas those at the back respond to bitter tastes.

cards.title: 7.1.4 The Eye
body: Human eyes are situated in the eye sockets of the skull.
The sockets give protection to the eyes.
A number of muscles hold the eyes in place, enabling them to move in different directions.
The front of the eyeball is covered by a thin, transparent membrane, the conjunctiva.

cards.title: 7.1.5 The Ear
body: The ear is the sense organ that assists in hearing.
The external ear: The external ear consists of the pinna, auditory canal and eardrum (tympanum).
The pinna helps to direct sound waves into the auditory canal.
Glands in the walls of the auditory canal produce a waxy material.

cards.title: Worked from review
cards.problem: Which of the following structures acts as a thin, protective membrane covering the front of the eyeball and lining the eyelids?

steps.text: **Given:** Anatomical structures covering the anterior surface of the eye.

**Concepts:** The conjunctiva is a thin, transparent mucous membrane that covers the front of the eyeball (except the cornea) and lines the inner surface of the eyelids, providing protection and lubrication.
The cornea is transparent but is a structural layer focusing light.
The sclera is the white, tough outer coat.

cards.title: Worked from review
cards.problem: What is the primary function of the Eustachian tube in the human ear?

steps.text: **Given:** Anatomical structures of the middle ear.
**Concepts:** The Eustachian tube connects the middle ear cavity to the pharynx, allowing air to pass in and out to equalize pressure across the eardrum.
Sound amplification is done by the ossicles (malleus, incus, stapes).
Equalization of pressure prevents the eardrum from rupturing or dampening vibrations, which is mediated by the Eustachian tube.

cards.answer: Equalization of air pressure on both sides of the tympanic membrane

cards.title: 7.2 The Internal Receptors
body: Receptors that receive information about internal body conditions are called internal receptors.
Organisms receive information about a stimulus or changes within their body with the help of these receptors.
Internal receptors detect stimuli related to muscle length and tension, limb position, pain, blood composition, blood volume, blood pressure, body temperature, etc.
Internal receptors can be classified as mechanoreceptors, thermoreceptors and chemoreceptors.
Mechanoreceptors are specialized receptors that monitor pressure, stretching, and bending forces.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which of the following structures acts as a thin, protective membrane covering the front of the eyeball and lining the eyelids?
cards.why:
**Given:** Anatomical structures covering the anterior surface of the eye.

**Concepts:** The conjunctiva is a thin, transparent mucous membrane that covers the front of the eyeball (except the cornea) and lines the inner surface of the eyelids, providing protection and lubrication.

**Steps:**
1. The cornea is transparent but is a structural layer focusing light.
2. The sclera is the white, tough outer coat.
3. The conjunctiva is the superficial mucous membrane that protects the cornea from friction.

**Final Result:** **Conjunctiva** is the correct structure.

glossary.meaning: A cataract: is an eye disease in which the lens becomes covered by an opaque film that affects sight, eventually causing total loss of sight.
Ossicles, which are the smallest bones in the human body, convert the sound waves striking the eardrum into mechanical vibrations.

tips.text: Humans are equipped with internal and external receptors that help them respond to changes in their body and the environment. These receptors are very important in the survival of the organism.
Some of the receptors form sense organs like the skin, nose, tongue, eye and ear. These sense organs respond to different stimuli in the environment.
The sense organs and stimuli they respond to are listed below.
Receptors which recognize different sensations, like pain, touch, pressure, etc. are present in the skin.
The nose is the sense organ where olfactory receptors are present.
Receptors, which recognize the primary tastes such as sweet, sour, bitter and salty, are present in the tongue.
The eye is the sense organ that helps us to see objects in our surroundings.
Images in the eye are formed on the retina, where rod and cone cells (the photoreceptors) are located.
The structures of the human ear assist in hearing sound.
The malfunctioning and non-functioning of sense organs are hazardous to one’s health. Therefore, we should take precautions for their care and proper functioning.
